column2: But he went from the harbour along a rough path
up through wooded country over the heights, where Athena
had told him of the divine swineherd, who most of all cared
for his livelihood of the servants whom divine Odysseus had acquired.
Him he found sitting in the forecourt, where his courtyard
was built high, in a place with a wide view,
fair and great, with a circuit round; which the swineherd
himself had built for the swine, while his lord was away,
apart from his mistress and old Laertes,
with drawn stones, and he topped it with wild pear;
and outside he drove stakes all along on both sides,
thick and close, splitting the dark heart of oak;
and inside the courtyard he made twelve sties
near each other, as beds for the swine; and in each
fifty swine that lie on the ground were penned,
breeding females; and the males slept outside,
far fewer; for the godlike suitors kept diminishing them by eating,
since the swineherd was always sending in the best
of all the well-fed fat hogs;
and they numbered three hundred and sixty.
And beside them four dogs, like wild beasts, always slept,
which the swineherd, leader of men, had reared.
He himself was fitting sandals about his feet,
cutting a well-coloured ox-hide; and the others
were away, one this way, one that, with the herded swine,
the three; and the fourth he had sent to the city,
to take a hog to the overbearing suitors under compulsion,
that sacrificing it they might sate their hearts with meat.
Suddenly the loud-barking dogs saw Odysseus.
They ran at him baying; but Odysseus
sat down with cunning, and the staff fell from his hand.
There he would have suffered shameful pain at his own farmstead;
but the swineherd, following quickly with swift feet,
rushed through the doorway, and the leather fell from his hand.
He shouted at the dogs and drove them one this way, one that,
with thick showers of stones; and he said to his lord:

Old man, the dogs very nearly tore you to pieces
38	suddenly, and you would have poured shame upon me.
39	And the gods have given me other pains and groans too;
40	for mourning and grieving for my godlike lord
41	I sit, and rear fat swine for others
42	to eat; while he, longing perhaps for food,
43	wanders over the land and city of men of foreign speech,
44	if indeed he still lives and sees the light of the sun.
45	But follow, let us go to the hut, old man, so that you too,
46	when you have sated your heart with bread and wine,
47	may tell from where you are and how many troubles you endured.
So saying, the divine swineherd led him to the hut,
and brought him in and seated him, and strewed thick brushwood,
and spread over it the skin of a shaggy wild goat,
his own bedding, great and shaggy. And Odysseus was glad
that he received him so, and spoke a word and addressed him:

May Zeus give you, stranger, and the other immortal gods,
54	what you most wish, because you received me readily.
And answering him you said, swineherd Eumaeus:

Stranger, it is not right for me, not even if one worse than you came,
57	to dishonour a stranger; for from Zeus are all
58	strangers and beggars; and a gift, small and dear,
59	is what we give; for that is the way of servants,
60	always fearful, when young lords
61	are in power. Indeed the gods bound the return of him
62	who would have loved me with care and given me possessions,
64	a house and a plot of land and a much-wooed wife,
63	such things as a kindly lord gives to his servant,
65	one who has toiled much for him, and a god prospers the work,
66	as this work too prospers for me, at which I abide.
67	So my lord would have benefited me much, if he had grown old here;
68	but he has perished—would that the whole race of Helen had perished
69	utterly, since she loosened the knees of many men;
70	for he too went for the honour of Agamemnon
71	to Ilios of the fine horses, to fight with the Trojans.
So saying, he quickly gathered his tunic with a belt,
and went to the sties, where the broods of piglets were penned.
Taking two from there he brought them and sacrificed both,
singed them and cut them up and pierced them on spits.
And roasting it all he brought and set before Odysseus
hot on the very spits; and he sprinkled white barley;
and in a wooden bowl he mixed honey-sweet wine,
and himself sat opposite, and urging him spoke:

Eat now, stranger, what is available for servants,
81	piglets; but the fat swine the suitors eat,
82	not thinking in their minds of any watching gods nor of pity.
83	Truly the blessed gods do not love cruel deeds,
84	but honour justice and the righteous works of men.
85	Even hostile and lawless men, who come upon a foreign
86	land and Zeus gives them plunder,
87	and having filled their ships they set out to go home,
88	even on them a strong fear of vengeance falls in their hearts.
89	But these know something, and have heard some voice from a god,
90	of that man's grievous destruction, since they are unwilling to woo
91	justly or to go back to their own, but at ease
92	devour his goods insolently, and there is no sparing.
93	For as many nights and days as come from Zeus,
94	never do they sacrifice one victim, nor only two;
95	and wine they waste insolently, drawing it off.
96	For his livelihood was boundless; not any
97	of the hero men had so much, either on the dark mainland
98	or on Ithaca itself; not even twenty men together
99	have so much wealth; and I shall tell you.
100	Twelve herds on the mainland; as many flocks of sheep,
101	as many droves of swine, as many wide herds of goats
102	feed there, strangers and his own herdsmen.
103	And here eleven wide herds of goats in all
104	graze at the far end, and good men watch over them.
105	From these each man daily drives in one animal for them,
106	whichever of the well-fed goats appears the best.
107	And I guard these swine and protect them,
108	and choose well the best of the swine and send it to them.
So he spoke, and he ate the meat with zeal and drank the wine
greedily and in silence, and devised evils for the suitors.
But when he had dined and satisfied his heart with food,
the other filled and gave him the cup from which he himself drank,
full of wine; and he took it, and was glad at heart,
and spoke to him winged words:

Friend, who was it that bought you with his possessions,
116	so very rich and mighty as you say?
117	You say he perished for the honour of Agamemnon.
118	Tell me, in case I may know such a man.
119	For Zeus perhaps knows this, and the other immortal gods,
120	whether I could give news of him, having seen him; for I have wandered much.
And then the swineherd, leader of men, answered him:

Old man, no wanderer who came
123	with news would persuade his wife and dear son,
124	but vagrants in need of care
125	lie idly, and are unwilling to tell the truth.
126	Whoever comes wandering to the land of Ithaca
127	goes to my mistress and speaks deceitful words;
128	and she receives him well and treats him kindly and asks each thing,
129	and for her lamenting tears fall from her eyelids,
130	as is right for a woman whose husband has perished elsewhere.
131	Quickly you too, old man, would fashion a tale,
132	if someone would give you a cloak and tunic as clothes.
133	But as for him, by now dogs and swift birds
134	are likely to have torn the skin from his bones, and his spirit has left him;
135	or the fishes ate him in the sea, and his bones
136	lie on the shore wrapped in much sand.
137	So he has perished there, and sorrows for his friends hereafter
138	for all, and for me most; for no other
139	kindly lord like him shall I find, wherever I go,
140	not even if I came again to the house of my father and mother,
141	where I was first born and they themselves reared me.
142	And yet not so much do I mourn for them any more, though I long
143	to see them with my eyes, being in my fatherland;
144	but longing for Odysseus who is gone seizes me.
145	Him, stranger, even though he is not here, I am ashamed
146	to name; for he loved me exceedingly and cared for me in his heart;
147	but I call him 'dear one', even though he is far away.
And again much-enduring divine Odysseus spoke to him:

Friend, since you utterly deny it, and say that he
150	will not come, and your heart is always unbelieving,
151	I shall not speak idly, but with an oath,
152	that Odysseus is returning; and let there be a reward for good news for me
153	at once, as soon as he comes to his own house:
154	clothe me in a cloak and tunic, fair garments;
155	before then, though I am in great need, I would not accept anything.
156	For hateful to me as the gates of Hades
157	is that man who, yielding to poverty, speaks deceitful words.
158	Let Zeus be witness first of the gods, and the hospitable table,
159	and the hearth of blameless Odysseus, to which I have come,
160	that all this shall be fulfilled as I say.
in this very lunar cycle Odysseus will come here.
With the old moon waning, and the new one rising,
he will return home, and will punish whoever here
dishonours his wife and glorious son."
And answering him you said, swineherd Eumaeus:

Old man, neither shall I pay this reward for good news,
167	nor will Odysseus ever come to his house; but drink
168	at ease, and let us turn to other things, and do not remind me
169	of these; for my heart within my breast
170	grieves, whenever anyone mentions my kindly lord.
171	But as for the oath, we shall let it be, and Odysseus
172	may he come as I wish, and Penelope
173	and old Laertes and godlike Telemachus.
174	Now again I mourn without ceasing for the son born to Odysseus,
175	Telemachus; whom, when the gods had reared him like a sapling,
176	I said he would be among men no worse
177	than his dear father, wondrous in form and looks;
178	but some one of the immortals, or some man, harmed his balanced
179	wits within; and he went to hear news of his father
180	to holy Pylos; and the proud suitors
181	lie in wait for him as he goes home, so that the race
182	of godlike Arceisius may perish nameless from Ithaca.
183	But of him we shall let be, whether he is caught
184	or escapes and the son of Kronos holds his hand over him.
185	But come, you, old man, tell me your own troubles
186	and tell me this truly, that I may know well:
187	who are you among men, and from where? Where is your city and parents?
188	On what ship did you come? And how did sailors
189	bring you to Ithaca? Who did they claim to be?
190	For I do not think you came here on foot.
And answering him wise Odysseus said:

Well then, I shall tell you these things very exactly.
193	If only there were for us two for a time food
194	and sweet wine inside the hut,
195	to feast quietly, and others to go to the work;
196	then easily I could not even in a whole year
197	finish telling the troubles of my heart,
198	all that I have toiled through by the will of the gods.
199	I claim descent from broad Crete,
200	the son of a rich man; and many other
201	sons were reared and born in the hall,
202	legitimate, from his wife; but a bought mother bore me,
203	a concubine, yet Castor son of Hylax honoured me equal to the lawful ones,
204	from whom I claim to be descended,
205	who then among the Cretans was honoured like a god in the land
206	for his prosperity and wealth and glorious sons.
207	But the fates of death came bearing him
208	to the house of Hades; and his proud sons
209	divided his livelihood and cast lots for it,
210	but to me they gave very little and allotted a dwelling.
211	Yet I took a wife from men of many estates
212	for my valour, since I was not a weakling
213	nor a flinch-from-war; now all has left me;
214	but nevertheless, looking at the stubble, I think you
215	can recognize it; for indeed very great misery holds me.
216	Truly Ares and Athena gave me boldness
217	and the power to break ranks; whenever I chose for an ambush
218	the best men, devising evils for the enemy,
219	never did my proud heart foresee death,
220	but leaping out far the first I took with my spear
221	whichever of the enemy yielded to me with his feet.
222	Such I was in war; but work was not dear to me
223	nor household care, which rears splendid children,
224	but ships with oars were always dear to me,
225	and wars and polished javelins and arrows,
226	grievous things, which to others are shuddersome.
227	But what was dear to me was what a god put in my mind;
228	for different men delight in different works.
229	For before the sons of the Achaeans set foot on Troy
230	nine times I led men and swift-going ships
231	against foreign men, and very much fell to me.
232	From these I picked what I liked, and afterwards much
233	I received by lot; and quickly my house grew, and then
234	I became dreaded and respected among the Cretans.
235	But when wide-seeing Zeus planned that hateful
236	expedition, which loosened the knees of many men,
237	then they bade me and famed Idomeneus
238	to lead the ships to Ilios; nor was there any way
239	to refuse, for harsh talk of the people held us.
240	There for nine years we sons of the Achaeans fought,
241	and in the tenth, having sacked the city of Priam, we went
242	home with our ships, and a god scattered the Achaeans.
243	But for me, wretched, counsel-wise Zeus devised evils;
244	for one month only I stayed, delighting in my children
245	and wedded wife and possessions; but then
246	my heart bade me sail to Egypt,
247	fitting out ships well with godlike comrades.
248	Nine ships I fitted out, and the people gathered quickly.
249	For six days then my trusty comrades
250	feasted; and I provided many victims
251	for sacrificing to the gods and for preparing a feast for themselves.
252	On the seventh we embarked and left broad Crete
253	and sailed with the North wind, a fair breeze,
254	easily, as if down a stream; and none of my
255	ships was harmed, but unscathed and without sickness
256	we sat, and the wind and the helmsmen steered them.
257	On the fifth day we came to the fair-flowing Egypt,
258	and I stopped the curved ships in the river Egypt.
259	There indeed I bade my trusty comrades
260	stay there by the ships and guard the ships,
261	and I urged scouts to go to the lookouts;
262	but they, yielding to insolence, following their own strength,
263	at once began to ravage the very beautiful fields of the Egyptian men,
264	and carried off women and infant children,
265	and killed the men; and soon the cry reached the city.
266	And they, hearing the shout, came at dawn
267	appearing; and the whole plain was filled with foot-soldiers and horses
268	and the flashing of bronze; and Zeus who delights in thunder
269	cast evil panic on my comrades, nor did any dare
270	to stand firm to face them; for evils stood round on every side.
271	There they killed many of us with the sharp bronze,
272	and others they led up alive to work for them under compulsion.
273	But in my mind Zeus himself put this thought—
274	would that I had died and met my fate
275	there in Egypt; for still woe awaited me—
276	at once I took the well-made helmet off my head
277	and the shield from my shoulders, and threw the spear out of my hand;
278	and I went up to the king's horses
279	and kissed and clasped his knees; and he saved me and pitied me,
280	and set me in a chariot and took me home weeping.
281	Indeed very many rushed at me with ash spears,
282	eager to kill me—for they were exceedingly angry—
283	but he held them off, and respected the wrath of Zeus,
284	god of guests, who is most angry at evil deeds.
285	There I stayed for seven years, and gathered much
286	wealth among the Egyptian men; for all gave.
287	But when the eighth year came round for me,
288	then there came a Phoenician man skilled in deceits,
289	a trickster, who had done many evils to men;
290	who led me away, persuading me with his mind, until we came to
291	Phoenicia, where his house and possessions lay.
292	There I stayed with him for a full year.
293	But when the months and days were completed,
294	as the year came round again and the seasons came on,
295	he put me on a sea-going ship for Libya,
296	devising lies, that I might go with him with the cargo,
297	but there he would sell me and take an immense price.
298	I followed him on the ship, suspecting it, yet under compulsion.
299	And she ran with the North wind, a fair breeze,
300	in the middle above Crete; and Zeus devised destruction for them.
301	But when we left Crete, and no other
302	land appeared, but heaven and sea,
303	then the son of Kronos set a dark cloud
304	over the hollow ship, and the sea grew dark beneath it.
305	And Zeus thundered at once and hurled a thunderbolt at the ship;
306	and she shook all over, struck by the thunderbolt of Zeus,
307	and was filled with sulphur; and all fell from the ship.
308	And they like sea-crows around the black ship
309	were carried on the waves; and the god took away their return.
310	But for me Zeus himself, though I had pains in my heart,
311	put into my hands the mast, huge, of the dark-prowed ship,
312	that I might yet escape woe.
313	Clinging to it I was carried by the baleful winds.
314	For nine days I was carried, and on the tenth black night
315	a great wave rolling brought me to the land of the Thesprotians.
316	There the king of the Thesprotians, the hero Pheidon,
317	took me in without ransom; for his dear son came upon me
318	overcome by cold and weariness, and led me to his house,
319	raising me by the hand, until he came to his father's halls;
320	and he clothed me about in a cloak and tunic as garments.
321	There I heard of Odysseus; for he said
322	that he had entertained and befriended him as he went to his fatherland,
323	and he showed me the possessions that Odysseus had gathered,
324	bronze and gold and much-wrought iron.
325	And it would feed another man even to the tenth generation,
326	so many treasures lay for that lord in the halls.
327	He said Odysseus had gone to Dodona, to hear from the god's
328	high-crested oak the counsel of Zeus,
329	how he might return to the rich land of Ithaca
330	after being so long away, openly or secretly.
331	And he swore to me himself, pouring a libation in his house,
332	that the ship was launched and the comrades were ready
333	who would send him to his dear fatherland.
334	But he sent me off first; for a ship of Thesprotian men
335	happened to be going to Dulichium, rich in grain.
336	There he bade them send me to king Acastus
337	with care; but an evil plan pleased them in their minds
338	concerning me, that I might yet utterly come to the woe of misery.
339	But when the sea-going ship had sailed far from the land,
340	at once they contrived for me the day of slavery.
341	They stripped me of my cloak and tunic as garments,
342	and threw about me another foul rag and tunic,
343	tattered, which you yourself see before your eyes;
344	and in the evening they reached the fields of clear-seen Ithaca.
345	There they bound me in the well-benched ship
346	with a well-twisted rope, tightly, and themselves disembarked
347	and hastily took their supper by the shore of the sea.
348	But the gods themselves loosened the bond for me
349	easily; and covering my head with the rag,
350	I slid down the polished rudder and laid my chest
351	to the sea, and then with both hands I paddled,
352	swimming, and very quickly I was out of their reach.
353	Coming up where there was a thicket of flowering wood,
354	I lay crouching. And they, groaning loudly,
355	went about; but since it did not seem to them better
356	to search further, they went back again
357	to the hollow ship; and the gods themselves hid me
358	easily, and brought me to the farmstead
359	of a knowing man; for it is still my fate to live.
And answering him you said, swineherd Eumaeus:

Ah, wretched stranger, you have greatly stirred my heart
362	telling each of these things, all you suffered and all your wanderings.
363	But in this I think it is not in order, and you will not persuade me
364	in what you say of Odysseus; why must you, being such,
365	lie idly? And I myself know well
366	about my lord's return, that he was hated by all the gods
367	utterly, because they did not subdue him among the Trojans
368	or in the hands of friends, when he had wound up the war.
369	Then all the Achaeans would have made him a tomb,
370	and he would have won great glory for his son hereafter;
371	but now the Harpies have snatched him away without glory.
372	But I live apart by the swine; and I do not go to the city,
373	unless wise Penelope somewhere
374	bids me come, when news comes from somewhere.
375	But they sit by and question about each thing,
376	both those who grieve for the lord long gone,
377	and those who rejoice in devouring his livelihood unpunished;
378	but to me it is not dear to inquire and ask,
379	since an Aetolian man deceived me with his story,
380	who having killed a man and wandered over much land
381	came to my house; and I treated him kindly.
382	He said he had seen him among the Cretans, with Idomeneus,
383	mending his ships, which the storms had shattered;
384	and he said he would come either in summer or in harvest,
385	bringing much wealth, with his godlike comrades.
386	And you, old man of many sorrows, since a spirit has brought you to me,
387	do not please me with lies nor charm me;
388	for it is not for this that I shall respect or befriend you,
389	but fearing Zeus, god of guests, and pitying you myself.
And answering him wise Odysseus said:

Truly you have an unbelieving heart in your breast,
392	such that not even with an oath have I won you over or persuaded you.
393	But come now, let us make an agreement; and behind it
394	the gods who hold Olympus shall be witnesses to us both.
395	If your lord comes back to this house,
396	clothe me in cloak and tunic and send me
397	to go to Dulichium, where it is dear to my heart;
398	but if your lord does not come as I say,
399	set your servants on me to throw me down from a great rock,
400	so that another beggar too may beware of deceiving.
And answering him the divine swineherd said:

Stranger, so indeed good fame and virtue would be mine
403	among men both at once and afterwards,
404	if I, having brought you to the hut and given you hospitality,
405	should then kill you and take away your dear life;
406	readily indeed then should I pray to Zeus son of Kronos.
407	But now it is the hour for supper; may my comrades soon
408	be inside, so that we may prepare a pleasant supper in the hut.
So they spoke such things to one another,
and close by came the swine and the men, the swineherds.
They shut them to sleep in their pens,
and an endless noise rose from the swine as they were penned.
And the divine swineherd called to his comrades:

Bring the best of the swine, that I may sacrifice for the stranger
415	from far away; and we ourselves too shall benefit, we who have long
416	suffered misery because of the white-tusked swine;
417	while others eat our labour unpaid.
So speaking he split wood with the pitiless bronze,
and they brought in a very fat boar of five years.
They stood it at the hearth; nor did the swineherd
forget the immortals; for he was of good mind;
but he, beginning the rite, threw into the fire hairs from the head
of the white-tusked boar, and prayed to all the gods
that wise Odysseus might return to his house.
And he struck, rising up, with a billet of oak, which he had left when splitting;
and the life left it. And they slaughtered and singed it,
and quickly cut it up; and the swineherd laid raw pieces,
beginning with all the limbs, in the rich fat,
and these he threw into the fire, sprinkling them with barley meal,
and they cut up the rest and pierced it on spits,
and roasted it carefully and drew all off,
and threw it heaped on the tables; and the swineherd
stood to carve; for he knew right shares in his mind.
And he divided it all in seven parts, cutting it up;
one he set for the nymphs and for Hermes, son of Maia,
with prayer, and the others he distributed to each;
and Odysseus he honoured with the long chine
of the white-tusked boar, and exalted the heart of his lord;
and wise Odysseus spoke to him and said:

Eumaeus, may you be as dear to father Zeus
441	as you are to me, since you honour such a man as I am with good things.
And answering him you said, swineherd Eumaeus:

Eat, strange stranger, and take pleasure in these things,
444	such as there are; and a god will give one thing and let another go,
445	whatever he wishes in his heart; for he can do all things.
He spoke, and sacrificed the first portions to the gods who are for ever,
and pouring a libation of gleaming wine he put the cup
into the hands of Odysseus, sacker of cities; and he sat by his portion.
And Mesaulius distributed bread to them, whom the swineherd
himself had acquired alone while his lord was away,
apart from his mistress and old Laertes;
he bought him from the Taphians with his own possessions.
And they put out their hands to the food ready laid before them.
But when they had put away desire for drink and food,
Mesaulius cleared away the bread, and they hastened to bed,
sated with bread and meat.
And night came on, evil, moonless, and Zeus rained
all night long, and the great West wind blew, always wet.
And among them Odysseus spoke, testing the swineherd,
to see if somehow, stripping off his cloak, he would give it, or urge
one of the others, since he cared for him exceedingly:

Hear me now, Eumaeus and all you other comrades,
463	I shall speak a word, making a boast; for wine bids me,
464	foolish wine, which sets even a wise man to sing very loudly
465	and to laugh softly, and lets him dance,
466	and sends forth some word that were better unspoken.
467	But since I have cried out at first, I shall not hide it.
468	Would that I were young and my strength steadfast,
469	as when we prepared and led an ambush under Troy.
470	The leaders were Odysseus and Menelaus son of Atreus,
471	and with them I was third in command; for they themselves bade it.
472	But when we came to the city and the steep wall,
473	we round the town among the thick bushes,
474	among the reeds and the marsh, crouching beneath our arms,
475	lay. And night came on, evil, when the North wind had fallen,
476	freezing; and above snow came like hoar-frost,
477	cold, and ice gathered thick about our shields.
478	Then all the others had cloaks and tunics,
479	and slept at ease, their shoulders covered with shields;
480	but I, when I went, left my cloak with my comrades
481	in folly, since I did not think I should be cold at all,
482	but followed with only a shield and my shining belt.
483	But when it was the third part of the night, and the stars had turned,
484	then I spoke to Odysseus who was near
485	nudging him with my elbow; and he promptly listened:
486	'Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of many devices,
487	I shall no longer be among the living, but the cold
488	overcomes me; for I have no cloak; a god deceived me
489	into being in a tunic alone; now there is no escape.'
490	So I spoke, and he then thought out this plan in his heart,
491	such a man was he at counsel and at fighting;
492	and speaking in a low voice he said a word to me:
493	'Be silent now, lest any other of the Achaeans hear you.'
494	And he propped his head on his elbow and spoke:
495	'Hear, friends; a divine dream came to me in my sleep.
496	We have come very far from the ships; but let someone
497	go and tell Agamemnon son of Atreus, shepherd of the people,
498	whether he will urge more men to come from the ships.'
499	So he spoke, and Thoas, son of Andraemon, rose up
500	quickly, and put off his purple cloak,
501	and went running to the ships; and I in his garment
502	lay gladly, and golden-throned Dawn shone.
503	Would that I were so young now and my strength steadfast;
504	then someone of the swineherds in the farmsteads would give a cloak,
505	for both, out of friendship and respect for a good man;
506	but now they dishonour me, since I have bad clothes on my skin.
And answering him you said, swineherd Eumaeus:

Old man, the tale you have told is blameless,
509	and you have not yet spoken a word beyond measure or unprofitable;
510	therefore you will lack neither clothing nor anything else
511	that is fitting for a hard-pressed suppliant who meets us,
512	for now; but in the morning you will shake out your own rags.
513	For we do not have many cloaks and changes of tunics
514	here to put on, but one only for each man.
515	But when Odysseus's dear son comes,
516	he himself will give you cloak and tunic as garments,
517	and send you where your heart and spirit bid.
So saying he sprang up, and set a bed for him near the fire,
and threw on it the skins of sheep and goats.
There Odysseus lay down; and over him he threw a cloak,
thick and large, which lay by him as a change,
to put on whenever some terrible storm arose.
So Odysseus slept there, and beside him
the young men slept; but the swineherd did not
like a bed there, to sleep away from the swine,
but he went out and armed himself; and Odysseus was glad
that he cared so for his property while he was away.
First he threw a sharp sword about his stout shoulders,
and put about him a very thick cloak to keep off the wind,
and took up the skin of a great well-fed goat,
and took a sharp javelin, a defence against dogs and men.
And he went to lie where the white-tusked swine
slept under a hollow rock, in shelter from the North wind.
